items.title: Section: Refuting Rival Views — If a Name Really Matched Its Object, One Thing Would Have Countless, Contradictory Selves

items.zh: 若於諸法諸事隨起言說，即於彼法彼事有自性者，如是一法一事應有眾多自性。何以故？以於一法一事制立眾多假說而詮表故。
items.en: If, whenever speech arises regarding some phenomenon or event, that very phenomenon or event thereby possessed the nature asserted, then one single phenomenon or event ought to possess countless natures. Why is this? Because countless distinct designations are established to describe one single phenomenon or event.

items.zh: 亦非眾多假說詮表決定可得。謂隨一假說，於彼法彼事有體、有分、有其自性；非餘假說。是故一切假說若具不具，於一切法、於一切事，皆非有體、有分、有其自性。
items.en: Nor can it be determined that any of the many designations describing one thing is the correct one. That is to say: were it the case that some one particular designation genuinely possessed, for that phenomenon or event, a substance, a component, and a nature of its own that no other designation possessed — then, since every designation, whether complete or partial, applies equally to every phenomenon and every event, none of them could genuinely possess any substance, component, or nature of its own at all.

items.title: Section: Two More Contradictions — No-Substance and Non-Correspondence Close the Case Against Fixed Naming

items.zh: 又如前說色等諸法，若隨假說有自性者，要先有事，然後隨欲制立假說。先未制立彼假說時，彼法彼事應無自性；若無自性，無事制立假說詮表，不應道理；假說詮表既無所有，彼法彼事隨其假說而有自性，不應道理。
items.en: Moreover, regarding form and the other phenomena discussed earlier: if they possessed a nature only insofar as a designation is applied to them, then there must first be the event, and only afterwards, as desired, is a designation established for it. But before that designation was ever established, that phenomenon or event ought to have had no nature at all. And if it had no nature, then there would be no event for which to establish a designation describing it — which makes no sense. Since, in that case, the designation describing it would have nothing at all to rest on, to say that the phenomenon or event acquires a nature simply through its designation makes no sense either.

items.zh: 又若諸色未立假說詮表已前，先有色性，後依色性制立假說攝取色者，是則離色假說詮表，於色想法、於色想事應起色覺，而實不起。由此因緣由此道理，當知諸法離言自性。如說其色，如是受等如前所說乃至涅槃，應知亦爾。
items.en: Moreover, if form already possessed the nature of "form" prior to any designation being established describing it, and a designation were only afterwards established, on the basis of that nature, to describe form — then, apart from any designation describing form, the cognition "this is form" ought to arise merely with respect to something conceived of as form, or an event conceived of as form; yet in fact it does not arise. Just as with form, so too with feeling and the rest, up through nirvāṇa as discussed earlier — it should be understood that the same holds true.

items.title: Section: The Two Ways the Buddha's Teaching Gets Corrupted — Superimposition and Nihilistic Denial

items.zh: 有二種人，於佛所說法毘奈耶，俱為失壞。一者、於色等法、於色等事，謂有假說自性自相，於實無事起增益執。
items.en: There are two kinds of people who equally corrupt the Buddha's teaching of doctrine and discipline. The first, regarding form and other phenomena and events, holds that the imputed nature and characteristic asserted of them genuinely exists — generating a superimposing attachment towards what, in reality, has no such event at all.

items.zh: 二者、於假說相處、於假說相依離言自性勝義法性，謂一切種皆無所有，於實有事起損減執。
items.en: The second, regarding the ground on which the imputed characteristic arises and the basis on which it depends — the ultimate, inexpressible nature of phenomena — holds that this is entirely nonexistent in every respect, generating a denying attachment towards what, in reality, genuinely exists.

items.zh: 於實無事起增益執，妄立法者所有過失，已具如前顯了開示；於色等法實無事中，起增益執有過失故；於佛所說法毘奈耶甚為失壞。於色等法實有唯事起損減執壞諸法者所有過失，由是過失，於佛所說法毘奈耶甚為失壞，我今當說。謂若於彼色等諸法實有唯事起損減執，即無真實，亦無虛假。如是二種皆不應理。譬如要有色等諸蘊，方有假立補特伽羅，非無實事而有假立補特伽羅；如是要有色等諸法實有唯事，方可得有色等諸法假說所表，非無唯事而有色等假說所表。若唯有假，無有實事，既無依處，假亦無有，是則名為壞諸法者。

items.title: Section: "Nihilistic Emptiness" — When Misreading the Profound Sūtras Denies Everything at Once

items.zh: 如有一類，聞說難解大乘相應、空性相應、未極顯了密意趣義甚深經典，不能如實解所說義，起不如理虛妄分別。由不巧便所引尋思，起如是見，立如是論：一切唯假，是為真實，若作是觀名為正觀。
items.en: There is a certain kind of person who, upon hearing profound scriptures difficult to understand, connected with the Great Vehicle, connected with emptiness, and expressing a hidden intent not yet fully made explicit, fails to genuinely understand the meaning being taught, and instead gives rise to unreasonable, false discrimination ... generating a view of this kind, and establishing a thesis of this kind: "everything is merely imputation — this alone is true reality; and to view things this way is to view them correctly."

items.zh: 彼於虛假所依處所實有唯事，撥為非有，是則一切虛假皆無，何當得有一切唯假是為真實。由此道理，彼於真實及以虛假二種俱謗都無所有。由謗真實及虛假故，當知是名最極無者。
items.en: Such a person denies as nonexistent the genuinely-existing event on which imputation itself depends — but if that is denied, then imputation itself becomes entirely nonexistent too, and there could then be no basis at all for asserting "everything is merely imputation" as true. For this reason, such a person denies both true reality and imputed appearance alike as utterly nonexistent — and because both true reality and imputed appearance are denied, this should be recognised as the most extreme form of nihilism.

items.title: Section: Why Wisdom Practitioners Must Refuse to Debate the Nihilist — and the Buddha's Own Verdict on Which Error Is Worse

items.zh: 如是無者，一切有智同梵行者不應共語、不應共住。如是無者，能自敗壞，亦壞世間隨彼見者。
items.en: Towards such a nihilist, no wise fellow-practitioner should engage in conversation or dwell together with them. Such a nihilist destroys themselves, and also destroys anyone in the world who follows their view.

items.zh: 世尊依彼密意說言：寧如一類起我見者，不如一類惡取空者。何以故？起我見者，唯於所知境界迷惑，不謗一切所知境界；不由此因墮諸惡趣。
items.en: The World-Honoured One, with this specific intent in mind, said: "Better to be someone who holds a view of self than to be someone who has wrongly grasped emptiness." Why is this? One who holds a view of self is merely confused with respect to the object of knowledge, but does not deny the object of knowledge in every respect — and for this reason does not, on this account, fall into the miserable realms.

items.title: Six Further Reasons a Mere Self-View Never Destroys the Path

items.zh: 於他求法、求苦解脫不為虛誑，不作稽留；於法、於諦亦能建立；於諸學處不生慢緩。
items.en: Towards others who seek the teaching, or seek liberation from suffering, they are not deceptive and do not cause delay; they are also able to uphold the teaching and the truths; and they cause no slackening or delay regarding the trainings to be undertaken.

items.title: Section: Why Nihilistic Emptiness Is the Graver Error — The Full Reckoning

items.zh: 惡取空者，亦於所知境界迷惑，亦謗一切所知境界；由此因故，墮諸惡趣。於他求法、求苦解脫能為虛誑，亦作稽留；於法、於諦不能建立；於諸學處極生慢緩。如是損減實有事者，於佛所說法毘奈耶甚為失壞。
items.en: One who wrongly grasps emptiness is likewise confused with respect to the object of knowledge, but additionally denies the object of knowledge in every respect — and for this reason falls into the miserable realms. Towards others who seek the teaching, or seek liberation from suffering, they can become deceptive and cause delay; they are unable to uphold the teaching and the truths; and they cause great slackening and delay regarding the trainings to be undertaken. Such a person, who denies what genuinely exists, gravely corrupts the Buddha's teaching of doctrine and discipline.

blocks.text: Arguments against two errors: that words capture real natures, and that "emptiness" means nothing exists. The second, the treatise says, is worse. A short passage (0488b14) is untranslated.

"If, whenever speech arises about a phenomenon, that phenomenon thereby possessed the nature asserted, then a single phenomenon ought to possess countless natures, because countless designations describe one thing." Nor can one say which name is the right one.

"If things possessed a nature only insofar as a name is applied, then before the name was given, there would be no thing to name." And "if form already had the nature 'form' before any name, then without any name the cognition 'this is form' should arise". Neither works: names are imputed on things, but do not capture them.

subs.head: Two ways to corrupt the teaching

blocks.text: The first holds that "the imputed nature genuinely exists": superimposition. The second holds that "the ground on which imputation depends, the ultimate, inexpressible nature, is entirely nonexistent": denial.

Someone hears "profound scriptures connected with emptiness, expressing a hidden intent not yet made explicit", misunderstands, and concludes that everything is mere imputation and nothing exists. But "if the real event on which imputation depends is denied, imputation itself becomes nonexistent".

"Towards such a nihilist, no wise practitioner should converse or dwell." The Buddha said: "Better to hold a view of self than to wrongly grasp emptiness." One with self-view is confused about the object, "but does not deny it", does not deceive others, and can still uphold the truths; one who wrongly grasps emptiness denies everything, and "falls into the miserable realms".

quiz.q: "Whenever speech arises regarding phenomena (法) or events (事)." How does Master Cháng Bǎi distinguish them?
options: 法 is the sixth consciousness's object; 事 the conditioned things the five sense consciousnesses take
quiz.why: "If, whenever speech arises regarding some phenomenon or event, that very phenomenon or event thereby possessed the nature asserted, then one single phenomenon or event ought to possess countless natures." Master Cháng Bǎi: 法 is the object of the sixth consciousness; 事 is the conditioned things taken by the five sense consciousnesses.

quiz.q: "Without a nature, there'd be no event to designate — unreasonable." How does Venerable Miào Jìng put it?
options: no tree there, yet you say there's a tree — isn't that lying?
quiz.why: "And if it had no nature, then there would be no event for which to establish a designation describing it — which makes no sense." Venerable Miào Jìng: there's no tree there and you say there's a tree — isn't that deceiving people!

quiz.q: "Apart from the designation, the cognition 'form' should arise — but it doesn't." What does Master Cháng Bǎi say?
options: beings know things by names — without a name, the thing can't be recognised
quiz.why: "Then, apart from any designation describing form, the cognition 'this is form' ought to arise merely with respect to something conceived of as form … yet in fact it does not arise." Master Cháng Bǎi: beings recognise things by their names; without a name, they can't recognise the thing.

quiz.q: Two kinds of people "corrupt the Buddha's doctrine and discipline (毗奈耶)." How does Venerable Miào Jìng explain 毗奈耶 as "extinguishing"?
options: suffering comes from my inner afflictions, not from outside
quiz.why: "There are two kinds of people who equally corrupt the Buddha's teaching of doctrine and discipline." Venerable Miào Jìng: it's because I have afflictions inside that I suffer — not because of external causes. (毗奈耶 means extinguishing — extinguishing inner affliction.)

quiz.q: Some misunderstand profound scriptures "connected with emptiness." What does this especially refer to, per Master Cháng Bǎi?
options: especially the emptiness taught in the Prajñāpāramitā sūtras
quiz.why: "There is a certain kind of person who, upon hearing profound scriptures difficult to understand, connected with the Great Vehicle, connected with emptiness, and expressing a hidden intent not yet fully made explicit." Master Cháng Bǎi: it especially means the emptiness taught in the Prajñāpāramitā sūtras.

quiz.q: "Better to hold a view of self than to wrongly grasp emptiness" — rendered "a view of self." What is this view, per the lectures?
options: a view of a personal self
Cháng Bǎi: the view of a self in phenomena — taking imputed dharmas as real; Miào Jìng: better to think like the self-view holder
quiz.why: "The World-Honoured One, with this specific intent in mind, said: 'Better to be someone who holds a view of self than to be someone who has wrongly grasped emptiness.'" Master Cháng Bǎi: the self-view here is holding all imputed dharmas as real — the view of a self in phenomena. Venerable Miào Jìng: better to think like that kind of self-view holder. The English reading as a personal self doesn't match.

quiz.q: How many faults does the one who wrongly grasps emptiness have, per Master Cháng Bǎi?
quiz.why: "One who wrongly grasps emptiness is likewise confused with respect to the object of knowledge, but additionally denies the object of knowledge in every respect — and for this reason falls into the miserable realms." Master Cháng Bǎi: one who wrongly grasps emptiness has seven faults.
